title: Why some data is harder to collect than others
summary: The most useful data is often the least convenient to get: rare languages, specialist knowledge, real-world environments and behaviours that cannot be scraped or simulated easily.
body_markdown:
A lot of data looks abundant until you ask for something specific. There are billions of images online, but far fewer first-person videos of people carrying out the same household task from a consistent camera position. There is more speech than any model could listen to, but very little clean, consented audio from some dialects and languages. Expert knowledge exists everywhere, but much of it lives in people rather than in datasets.


That difference matters because the value of a dataset is often tied to the difficulty of collecting it. The harder the requirement is to satisfy, the less likely useful data already exists in the right form.


At Luel, this is where much of our collection work begins: with the parts of the world that are difficult to turn into structured, usable data.


## Scarcity is usually specific


A category can look well supplied while the data you actually need is scarce.


Speech is the clearest example. English audio is everywhere. English speech from a defined accent, age group, recording device and conversational setting is much harder to source. Move into a low-resource language and the problem compounds: fewer recordings, less transcription, fewer established corpora and often less agreement around spelling, dialect boundaries or written form.


The same applies to video. There is no shortage of video online, but a robotics team may need first-person footage of named actions, captured continuously, with hands visible and the surrounding environment in frame. Most existing video was never recorded for that purpose.


Data scarcity is therefore less about whether examples exist at all and more about whether they exist in the right conditions, with the right permissions and in a form a model can use.


## Some environments are difficult to reach


Useful data is often tied to a place.


A model operating in homes needs examples from real homes. A system used in warehouses, farms or streets needs data from those environments rather than a studio approximation. Geography can also matter for language, culture, infrastructure and device use.


Once collection leaves controlled settings, the operational difficulty rises. Contributors need to be found in the right locations, instructions have to work across different conditions and submissions need to remain consistent enough to combine.


This is part of what makes real-world collection valuable. Variation is not always a defect. Different lighting, rooms, phones, accents and behaviours can be the point of the dataset, provided the collection is designed to preserve the variation that matters.


## Expertise creates another bottleneck


Some data cannot be produced by just anyone.


A general contributor can record a conversation or photograph an object. A specialist evaluation might require a doctor, engineer, lawyer or fluent speaker of a particular dialect. The more knowledge a task requires, the smaller the pool of people who can complete it reliably.


Expert data is difficult for another reason: the useful signal is often judgement rather than raw content. Two specialists may disagree, and that disagreement can itself be meaningful. Collecting the answer is only part of the work; defining what counts as a good answer and how it should be evaluated matters just as much.


This is why expert datasets tend to be slower and more expensive to build. The scarce resource is not storage or compute. It is access to people with the right knowledge.


## Collection is only useful if the data survives review


Hard-to-source data becomes even harder when quality requirements are applied.


A recording in the right language is not useful if the wrong speaker completed the task. A first-person video may contain the right action but miss the important part of it. An expert response can still be unusable if the task was ambiguous or the annotation format does not capture the reasoning needed.


Quality assurance therefore has to be designed around the collection itself. The question is not whether a submission is generically "good," but whether it satisfies the requirements that made the data worth collecting in the first place.


That is especially important when the dataset contains variation by design. Background noise may be a defect in a clean voice corpus and useful signal in a production speech dataset. A collection process has to distinguish between unwanted noise and the real-world conditions the model is supposed to learn.


## The hardest data is often the most useful


The easiest data to collect is usually the data that already exists in abundance.


The difficult datasets are more often defined by a constraint: a language that is poorly represented, a behaviour that rarely appears online, a specialist group, a specific environment or a combination of conditions that no public dataset was built to capture.


That does not make every hard-to-collect dataset valuable. Difficulty only matters when it corresponds to something the model needs. But when an important capability is limited by missing data, collection becomes part of the research problem.


Luel's network of more than 900,000 contributors gives us a way to reach those gaps across languages, locations and modalities. The aim is not simply to collect more data, but to collect the data that is hardest to replace.
